en: I remember in my mind the infant Mukunda, reclining within the hollow of a banyan leaf, placing his lotus-foot upon his lotus-face with his lotus-hand. (1)

Having withdrawn the worlds into the interior of a banyan leaf, I remember in my mind Mukunda as a child—the Lord of all, who has descended for the welfare of all, whose form is devoid of beginning or end, and who lies there reclining. (2)

I remember in my mind the youthful Mukunda, whose limbs are as dark and tender as the blue lotus, whose lotus-feet are worshipped by Indra and the other gods, and who is the source of refuge for those who rely on the Santānaka and Kalpavṛkṣa trees. (3)

I remember in my mind the youthful Mukunda, with his long locks of hair, his dangling pearl necklace, his row of teeth marked by the playfulness of amorous grace, his bimba-fruit-like lips, and his beautiful, wide eyes. (4)

I remember Mukunda in my mind—how, after the mistress of the household had gone outside to fetch water, milk, and curds, she placed them on the carrying-sling, and he ate as much as he desired and feigned sleep by pretending to be a child. 5.

I remember in my mind the youthful Mukunda, who delights in dancing upon the surface of the hoods of Kāliya dwelling within the Yamunā; he has that serpent’s tail as his hand, and his face is like the autumnal moon. 6.

I remember in my mind the youthful Mukunda, whose noble heroism was bound within the mortar, who sported in the breaking of the pair of tall Arjuna trees, and whose beautiful eyes were as long as full-blown lotuses. 7.

I remember in my mind the child Mukunda—the Lord whose form is infinite, who consists of pure consciousness, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who, gazing with reverence at his mother’s face, drinks her breast milk. 8.
Thus ends the Bālamukundāṣṭaka in its entirety.
